client: I've been really struggling since my grandfather passed away last month. I can't stop thinking about all the times I was too busy to visit him, and now it's too late. The guilt keeps me up at night, and then during the day I just feel this heavy sadness that won't go away.
therapist: I hear how much pain you're carrying from losing your grandfather, and how those missed visits are weighing heavily on you right now. It makes complete sense that you'd be feeling this deep sadness and guilt during such a difficult loss. What would your grandfather say if he could see how much love and care you're holding for him now?

client:
I don't know what he'd say... that's kind of the problem. I keep imagining him being disappointed in me for not visiting more before he passed. I was so busy with work that last year, and now I can't stop thinking about all those times I put off seeing him. 

Sometimes I wonder if he understood how much I really loved him, or if he just thought I was making excuses. The guilt keeps me up at night.
therapist: It sounds like that painful question—whether he understood your love—keeps replaying in your mind, along with these images of him being disappointed. I wonder if we could gently explore other possible ways he might have viewed your relationship? What are some moments that showed the love between you two?

client: I keep trying to think of those good moments, but they get drowned out by the last time I saw him. I remember bringing him soup when he was sick, but then my brain just jumps to his face looking so hurt when we broke up. It’s like the bad stuff overshadows everything.
therapist: It makes sense that painful memories feel so loud right now—grief has a way of amplifying those difficult moments. Let's gently notice how your mind is focusing on that one expression, while the loving act of bringing soup shows care too. What would it feel like to hold both those truths—that relationships contain both beautiful and painful moments?

client: I get what you're saying about holding both truths, but the painful moments just seem to outweigh everything else right now. When I think about bringing the soup, all I can focus on is how they barely thanked me and then criticized me for not making it the "right" way. It's like the good things don't even count.
therapist: I hear how those critical moments feel so much heavier than the loving intentions behind your actions—it's like they erase the care you were trying to show. I wonder if we could explore what it might feel like to acknowledge that pain while also noticing that your effort to bring soup came from a place of love? What might it feel like to hold space for both those truths at once?

client:
I get what you're saying about holding both things at once, but it's hard. The guilt over my mom saying the soup was too salty just drowns out everything else. I keep replaying that moment and feeling like I failed her, even though I spent hours making it perfect. 

It's like my brain won't let me focus on the good intention part - that just feels like making excuses. Why can't I just get things right?
therapist: I hear how painful it is to feel like your efforts were overlooked, and how that moment has become a symbol of not being "enough"—that must feel so heavy. Our minds often fixate on perceived failures while minimizing our loving intentions—what would it feel like to recognize that both can be true: the disappointment happened, and your care was real too?

client:
I get what you're saying about recognizing both things can be true, but it's just... when I think about that moment, all I feel is the sting of rejection. Like my care didn't matter at all. I keep replaying their dismissive reaction in my head and it makes me feel so small. 

The idea that my intentions were good feels hollow when the outcome was so painful. How do I even begin to separate those things? It all just blends together into this awful feeling of failure.
therapist: It sounds like that moment of rejection still feels so raw and immediate—like the pain completely overshadows any other part of the experience. I wonder if we could gently explore what it might feel like to acknowledge that sting while also noticing that the depth of your hurt shows how deeply you cared? What comes up when you imagine holding space for both those truths?

client: It’s hard to even think about holding space for both things because the hurt just feels so overwhelming. I keep replaying the moment in my head, and it’s like I can’t escape the feeling that I wasn’t good enough. I guess I did care a lot, but that almost makes it worse—like I put so much into it and it still ended up this way.
therapist: I hear how the depth of your care makes the hurt feel even more piercing—like your love and effort somehow magnified the pain of that moment. That tension between how much you gave and how it was received must feel so agonizing to hold. What would it feel like to imagine that your grandfather might have carried his own complicated feelings in that moment, separate from your worth or love?

client: I get what you're saying about him having his own feelings, but it's hard not to take it personally. When he pushed me away like that, it just confirmed all my worst fears that I'm not good enough for the people I love. Even if he was struggling with his own stuff, why did it have to come out as rejecting me?
therapist: I hear how deeply personal that rejection felt—like it tapped into your deepest fears about not being worthy of love. It makes complete sense that his reaction would hurt so profoundly when it seemed to confirm those painful beliefs about yourself. What would it feel like to consider that his ability to receive love might have been limited by his own struggles, rather than by your worth?

client: I can see what you're saying about his struggles, but it’s hard not to take it personally. I keep thinking, "If I were enough, he would have stayed." It feels like I’m just trying to make excuses for him instead of facing the truth—that maybe I’m the problem. I don’t know how to stop feeling that way.
therapist: I hear how deeply this belief—"if I were enough, he would have stayed"—has taken root, and how it feels like acknowledging his struggles might just be avoiding the "truth" about yourself. That self-blame must feel so heavy to carry. What would it feel like to consider that love and worthiness aren't conditional—that someone's capacity to receive love doesn't define your ability to give it?

client: It’s hard to accept that idea because it feels like if I were truly enough, he wouldn’t have left. I know you’re saying his struggles aren’t about me, but it’s hard not to take it personally—like I wasn’t worth sticking around for. Even though part of me wants to believe love isn’t conditional, it feels like the evidence in my life says otherwise.
therapist: I hear how deeply this belief—"if I were enough, he wouldn’t have left"—feels tied to your lived experiences, and how hard it is to separate his actions from your worth. That struggle to hold onto the idea of unconditional love, especially when it feels contradicted by past experiences, must feel so painful. What might it feel like to gently explore what "enough" means to you, and whether you’re holding yourself to a standard no one could ever meet?
